It's understandable to feel nervous. Choosing a career can seem like choosing the shape of your whole life, but it usually isn't a one-time, irreversible decision. People change roles, industries, and priorities, and what suits you can change as you do.

You also don't have to discover one perfect calling before you can move forward. Aim for a reasonable next step: work that meets your needs, uses some of your strengths, or helps you learn what you want more of. A career can be worthwhile because it offers stability, good colleagues, useful skills, or time for interests outside work - not because it feels like a lifelong passion.

Try replacing "What career suits me?" with smaller questions: What kinds of tasks do I enjoy or dislike? What conditions matter to me - income, flexibility, security, purpose, location? What am I curious enough to test? Then gather evidence through a short course, a project, volunteering, a part-time role, or conversations with people doing the work. Small experiments are less daunting than trying to think your way to certainty.

It may help to set a time limit for exploring and a date to make a practical decision, knowing you can review it later. You don't need complete confidence; you need enough information to take the next step. If the anxiety is making it hard to sleep, function, or make any decision, talking it through with a trusted person or career adviser can help.

response_text:
You do not need a long work history to apply for a first job. "Experience preferred" is often a wish list, not a strict requirement, especially for entry-level roles. Look for openings that mention training, seasonal work, or no experience required, and consider places such as grocery stores, restaurants, movie theaters, recreation programs, and local shops. You can also ask nearby businesses whether they hire 16-year-olds, even if they have no listing.

Keep your résumé to one page. Put your name and professional contact information at the top, followed by a short summary such as "Reliable high school student seeking a part-time position; available evenings and weekends." Include your education, expected graduation date, relevant skills, and any activities or responsibilities that show reliability, teamwork, communication, or initiative. School projects, clubs, sports, volunteering, babysitting, tutoring, and helping with family responsibilities can all count if you describe what you actually did. For example, "Tutored a younger student in math weekly" is more useful than simply listing "math." Don't invent experience or overstate your skills, and leave off your age, photo, and personal details such as your full street address.

For references, ask adults who know you in a responsible setting - a teacher, coach, volunteer supervisor, or family friend you have worked with. Ask permission first, and provide their contact details only when requested. If you have no references yet, volunteering or helping with a school or community activity can help you build one.

Check your local rules for working minors: permitted hours, required work permits, and limits on particular tasks vary by location. Be clear about your availability, arrive on time, and follow up politely after applying. A first job is mainly a chance to demonstrate dependability and learn; you are not expected to arrive as a trained professional.
